summary: Runnable and interpretable from one check run because only the pooler path changes, the branch is on T only, and prepare() prints the per-T winner table; but the mechanism is weaker than stated (nvjet 128xT '4x1 splitK' already runs a 4-way split-K over ~128 CTAs, the practical H200 skinny-GEMM ceiling measured on bf16_proj is 3.3-3.6 TB/s, and the layer-level gain is capped by the side-stream router slack of ~5-7 us), so expect neutral-to-small, with the honest readout in the per-shape sliding decode_16/32 rows and the printed table rather than the headline.
justification: Profile support: in the best run (job 5755a412dda244a1) the pooler is nvjet_sm90_tst_128x16_64x11_4x1_v_bz_splitK_TNT 20.3 us at T=16 and 128x32 20.8 us at T=32, plus a cublasLt splitKreduce ~2 us, against a 14.0 us floor for the 67 MB weight stream (3.3-3.5 TB/s achieved), so the ~7 us gap per shape is real. But three things shrink it. (1) The '4x more CTAs' claim is not a difference from today: the nvjet kernel's name says splitK with a 4x1 layout, i.e. cuBLAS already splits K four ways and reduces in a second kernel; a torch.bmm over S=4 K-chunks with fp32 partials plus a torch.sum reproduces the same CTA count, the same weight traffic and the same reduce round-trip, just with cuBLAS's batched heuristic choosing the tile instead of its split-K heuristic. The only genuinely different candidate is S=2. (2) bf16_proj's pooler-triton-skinny-m32 (job 9f0ad00bbc874d31) measured a plain full-K stream at 20.2 us = 3.3 TB/s and nvjet at 3.4-3.6 TB/s; nothing yet has pushed this shape past ~3.6 TB/s on H200, so the realistic saving is 0-3 us, not 7. (3) In the layer, the pooler overlaps the router hi/lo pair (nvjet tss 64x16 splitK 9.3 us for 2 calls) + add + FusedMuseSparkRouting on the side stream, joined before the experts; the critical path is max(pooler ~22, side ~14-17), so even a perfect pooler can only recover the ~5-7 us slack, and extra CTAs contend with the side stream's kernels. Net: ~1-2% on sliding decode_16/32 (262-265 us), <1% on the full decode_16/32 shapes (440-615 us) which the 'faster' globs also cover but which will read flat regardless, and ~0.3% on the geomean. Shapes/directions vs TASK.md are otherwise consistent: T table {1,8,16,32,128,256} covers all six loads; decode_1 and verify_32 flat are right; the expected list omits verify_1 (T=8, same regime as T=16, should be faster-or-flat) and verify_16 (T=128, should be flat), both of which the table does tune. Candidate (b) F.linear is dead weight: bf16_proj's parity review established that _bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl resolves to the same cuBLAS TN kernel as x @ w.T on H200. Weakest link: the hypothesis assumes split-K adds parallelism cuBLAS lacks, when cuBLAS is already split-K here; the run really tests whether cuBLAS's batched-GEMM kernel choice for [T,2048]x[2048,4096] streams faster than its split-K choice for [T,8192]x[8192,4096], which is an empirical coin flip with a 2-3 us ceiling.
confounders: sglang-pipeline-parity-router-hilo-m8 (router GEMM, landed): it moved T=8's side-stream router from the 26 us fp32 SIMT path (which overran the 21 us pooler, making the pooler irrelevant to verify_1's critical path) to the hi/lo bf16 pair (~15 us + routing, now hidden under the pooler with ~3-5 us slack). So any verify_1 gain from a faster pooler exists only because of that landed change, and is capped at that slack; at T=16/32 the hi/lo path is SGLang's own and unchanged by the landing, but the same max(pooler, side-branch) ceiling and SM contention with the side stream apply. This conditions the size of the effect, not its sign or attribution, and reverting it would only hide the pooler behind the slower router at T=8, so no A/B is needed.
interference: No companion is warranted. A gain is unambiguous: the only changed code path is the pooler GEMM at the tabled T values, the branch is shape-only, and prepare() prints which form each T picked, so a per-shape gain pairs directly with a non-default pick. A loss is attributable too: a loss with (c)/(d) chosen means the isolated-winner split-K is worse in situ (side-stream contention or the extra sum launch), which is the mechanism-level answer. A flat result with (a) chosen everywhere means split-K never beat nvjet even in isolation; a flat result with (c)/(d) chosen on the sliding decode shapes means the isolated saving did not survive the max(pooler, router) critical path or was below ~1%, and either reading closes the question for this area. ab-revert of the landed hypothesis is pointless (it only makes the T=8 pooler invisible); ab-tune has no tunable that touches the pooler; a forced-(a) control is byte-for-byte the base kernel_fn and would be a wasted run. The one refinement worth noting as a follow-up, not a companion, is an in-situ autotune (time each candidate with the router hi/lo + routing running on the side stream as kernel_fn does) if the table picks (c)/(d) but the rows stay flat.
rules_flags: Autotune runs in prepare() (untimed, 300 s, called once per run per the technical rules) using torch.cuda.graph capture/replay and CUDA events on synthetic inputs: not a timed-call host sync and not a harness timing patch, so allowed; it must free the graphs, the private mempools, the L2-flush buffer and the synthetic inputs before returning, restore the current stream, and never keep anything derived from data (prepare never sees data, so only the weight chunk copy and the integer winner table may persist).

Precision: fp32 bmm partials summed in fp32 and rounded to bf16 once is equal-or-finer than cuBLAS's single rounding, and the [S, K/S, 4096] chunk copy is a lossless bf16 relayout, both allowed. Do NOT fall back to bf16 partials (torch.bmm without out_dtype then .float().sum()) if out_dtype is unsupported on bmm in the judge's torch: four bf16-rounded partials are coarser than SGLang's path. torch.mm(out_dtype=float32) is proven on the judge (used by master); bmm's out_dtype cannot be verified from this node, so the implementer should guard with a try at prepare() time and drop candidates (c)/(d) rather than degrade.

The 'x viewed as [S, T, 8192/S]' must be x.view(T, S, 8192 // S).transpose(0, 1) (strided batch, no copy); x.view(S, T, 8192 // S) is a silent wrong-chunking that the judge would fail on, costing the run.

Branching is on cfg['tokens'] only, the table covers exactly the scored T values and defaults to (a) elsewhere, so the 13 correctness tests (which include T=8, 16 and 264) exercise the tuned path at T=8/16 and the nearby-shape reruns in final review stay on cuBLAS. No every-key or caching concerns: the change touches no attention and no input-derived state.

Determinism across the final-review reruns: an autotune with a hair-thin margin could flap between (a) and (c)/(d) across runs and add variance; require a non-default pick to beat (a) by a margin (e.g. >= 3% or >= 0.5 us median over the 50 replays) and print both medians, so a rerun of the same code reproduces the same table.
open_questions: Does torch.bmm accept out_dtype=torch.float32 in the judge's PyTorch build? master's torch.mm(out_dtype=) works there; if bmm does not, candidates (c)/(d) vanish and the run degenerates to the base.

Which cuBLAS kernel does the batched [T, 2048] x [2048, 4096] GEMM pick, and with what layout? Storing chunks as [S, 2048, 4096] (K-major rows) gives cuBLAS an NN operand instead of the TN layout nvjet currently uses; consider adding the [S, 4096, 2048] + transpose(1, 2) layout as a candidate, since layout can change the kernel family as much as S does.

Expected list omits verify_1 (T=8) and verify_16 (T=128) although both are tabled; add them (faster-or-flat and flat) so the attribution grid is complete, and expect the full decode_16/32 shapes (440/615 us) to read flat even on success since the pooler is 3-5% of them.

Record in FINDINGS, from the profile, the achieved TB/s of whatever bmm kernel the autotune selects (67 MB / kernel us): the skinny-GEMM family on this problem (and bf16_proj's pooler-skinny-tiled-weight-layout) hinges on whether anything beats ~3.6 TB/s on H200 for this weight stream.

If the table picks (c)/(d) for T=16/32 but the sliding decode rows are flat, the next step is an in-situ autotune (candidates timed with the router hi/lo + routing on the side stream) rather than more split factors; if the table picks (a) everywhere, the area should go on the do-not-retry list for cuBLAS-level tricks and any further pooler work needs a different mechanism (e.g. overlapping the pooler with the unpooler/attention tail, not a faster stream).
